```{r}
#Import Dataset
student <- read.csv(file.choose())
View(student)
#install.packages("car")

#Display first 10 rows
head(student,10)

#Check the structure
str(student)

#Check the dimensions
dim(student)

#Check summary statistics
summary(student)

#Check missing values
colSums(is.na(student))

#Check duplicate rows
sum(duplicated(student))

#HANDLING DUPLICATES

# Create a cleaned dataset by removing duplicates
student_clean <- student[!duplicated(student), ]

# Check the new dimensions
dim(student_clean)

# Confirm that duplicates have been removed
sum(duplicated(student_clean))

# Convert extracurricular activities Variable into a factor as it is categorical, not continuous numerical measurement.

student_clean$Extracurricular.Activities <- as.factor(
  student_clean$Extracurricular.Activities
)

# Check the variable type
str(student_clean)

# Count students in each category
table(student_clean$Extracurricular.Activities)

#Before multiple linear regression,First we look for the relationships between our variables.

# Check the distribution of student performance

hist(student_clean$Performance.Index,
     main = "Distribution of Student Performance",
     xlab = "Performance Index",
     col = "lightblue",
     border = "black")

# Calculate the average performance
mean(student_clean$Performance.Index)

# Calculate the median performance
median(student_clean$Performance.Index)

# Calculate the standard deviation
sd(student_clean$Performance.Index)

# Scatter plots for numeric predictors
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(student_clean$Hours.Studied, student_clean$Performance.Index,
     xlab = "Hours Studied", ylab = "Performance Index",
     main = "Hours Studied", pch = 19, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.2))
abline(lm(Performance.Index ~ Hours.Studied, data = student_clean), col = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(student_clean$Previous.Scores, student_clean$Performance.Index,
     xlab = "Previous Scores", ylab = "Performance Index",
     main = "Previous Scores", pch = 19, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.2))
abline(lm(Performance.Index ~ Previous.Scores, data = student_clean), col = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(student_clean$Sleep.Hours, student_clean$Performance.Index,
     xlab = "Sleep Hours", ylab = "Performance Index",
     main = "Sleep Hours", pch = 19, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.2))
abline(lm(Performance.Index ~ Sleep.Hours, data = student_clean), col = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(student_clean$Sample.Question.Papers.Practiced, student_clean$Performance.Index,
     xlab = "Papers Practiced", ylab = "Performance Index",
     main = "Papers Practiced", pch = 19, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.2))
abline(lm(Performance.Index ~ Sample.Question.Papers.Practiced, data = student_clean), col = "red", lwd = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Categorical predictor: boxplot
boxplot(Performance.Index ~ Extracurricular.Activities, data = student_clean,
        xlab = "Extracurricular Activities", ylab = "Performance Index",
        main = "Performance by Extracurricular Activities", col = c("lightblue", "lightgreen"))

# Average performance by study hours
aggregate(Performance.Index ~ Hours.Studied, data = student_clean, FUN = mean)
num_vars <- student_clean[, c("Hours.Studied", "Previous.Scores", "Sleep.Hours",
                              "Sample.Question.Papers.Practiced", "Performance.Index")]
round(cor(num_vars), 3)

model <- lm(Performance.Index ~ Hours.Studied + Previous.Scores +
              Extracurricular.Activities + Sleep.Hours +
              Sample.Question.Papers.Practiced,
            data = student_clean)

summary(model)
confint(model)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Multicollinearity
library(car)      
vif(model)# As VIF values are approximately 1 which is below the commonly used threshold of 5,thus there is no evidence of problematic multicollinearity among the independent variables.

#Checking Independence of errors using Durbin-Watson test 
# Install the package
#install.packages("lmtest")

# Load the package
library(lmtest)

# Perform Durbin-Watson test
dwtest(model)
# Perform the Breusch-Godfrey test
bgtest(model, order = 1)

# CHECKING HOMOSCEDASTICITY

# Perform the Breusch-Pagan test
bptest(model)

# CHECKING MODEL SPECIFICATION

# Perform Ramsey RESET test
resettest(model)

# CHECKING INFLUENTIAL OBSERVATIONS

# Calculate Cook's Distance
cooks_distance <- cooks.distance(model)

# Plot Cook's Distance
plot(cooks_distance,
     type = "h",
     main = "Cook's Distance",
     ylab = "Cook's Distance",
     xlab = "Observation")

graphics.off()      
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
 par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
plot(Performance.Index ~ Hours.Studied, data = student_clean,
     pch = 19, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.2),
     xlab = "Hours Studied", ylab = "Performance Index",
     main = "Hours Studied")
abline(lm(Performance.Index ~ Hours.Studied, data = student_clean),
       col = "red", lwd = 2)
summary(model)
```
### Interpretation of Results

The multiple linear regression analysis revealed a strong positive relationship between student performance and the five selected independent variables: hours studied, previous scores, extracurricular activities, sleep hours, and sample question papers practiced.

All five predictors were statistically significant at the 5% significance level. The model achieved an R-squared of 98.87%, indicating that the selected variables explain a substantial proportion of the variation in student performance.

The diagnostic tests showed no evidence of problematic multicollinearity, positive autocorrelation, serial correlation up to order 1, or heteroscedasticity.

However, the Ramsey RESET test indicated a potential model specification problem, suggesting that further investigation into the functional form and possible nonlinear relationships is necessary.

Overall, the model demonstrates strong explanatory power and identifies important variables associated with student performance. Nevertheless, the specification issue should be investigated before the model is considered fully adequate for statistical inference or prediction.
